summary: PyroHarmonix is a WebGIS prototype that turns NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into an interactive activity calendar. Users select a region and year, process locally stored observations or request new FIRMS data with an estimated call count and duration, then explore detections aggregated by H3 cell and UTC day, monthly seasonality, historical comparisons when enough prior data exist, and downloadable CSV results. The project responds to the challenge of examining MODIS’s long archive alongside VIIRS’s newer, finer observations, helping researchers, land managers and emergency planners recognize seasonal patterns and unusual activity. A real Ribeirão Preto, Brazil, August 2024 case demonstrates the workflow. The repository includes an honest, reproducible but partial 2024 snapshot. Current data are uncalibrated; missing records do not imply absence of fire, and the prototype does not predict fires or map burned areas.
details:
PyroHarmonix is a containerized WebGIS built with Python/Django, React/JavaScript, PostgreSQL, Docker and Leaflet/OpenStreetMap. Users select a rectangular area and year, then either process stored observations or request a NASA FIRMS download with an estimated call count and duration. The backend preserves the original sensor records and aggregates MODIS and VIIRS detections by H3 resolution-8 cell and UTC day. When available, a monthly Brazil-wide MODIS/VIIRS factor is applied if both products meet a 500-detection threshold; overlapping counts are averaged, while single-sensor counts use the available source.

The interface provides an active-fire map, monthly seasonality, an annual calendar, historical median/anomaly comparisons when sufficient prior records exist, and CSV export. A real Ribeirão Preto case shows 12,476 equivalent detections for August 21–31, 2024. The repository also includes a partial 2024 CSV snapshot with 7,747 cell/day records summing to 12,535 equivalent detections. Those data are uncalibrated and incomplete. The tool is exploratory: it does not forecast fires, identify burned-area perimeters, or establish that missing records mean no fire. Its goal is to make satellite observations easier to explore while making data gaps and uncertainty visible.
